Evaluation of the HAL dynamic scheduler for concurrent multi-agent workloads. The upper panel shows per-agent HAL histories guiding drafting budget allocation. The lower panel demonstrates that the dynamic drafting budget allocation enables a higher throughput of a 1.12 × 1.12\times speedup over the static scheduling. Figure 14 . Execution trace of a three-agent workload. The synchronous baseline (upper) indicates the severe hardware idling induced by tool execution, while our asynchronous yielding (lower) allows pending agents to steal idle budgets via microsecond-level context switches, thereby reducing wall-clock time and elevating system throughput (right panels). Traditional speculative decoding frameworks inherently underutilize resources by rigidly partitioning compute among agents, regardless of their actual generation predictability. To expose this inefficiency, we evaluate the dynamic scheduler with three concurrent agents, where each agent’s task is randomly sampled from the mixed dataset, thereby exhibiting differences in drafting difficulty. As shown in the execution trace of Figure 13 , the system continuously monitors each agent’s Historical Accepted Length (HAL) using an exponential moving average. When an agent exhibits a sustained high acceptance trend, the scheduler reduces the draft budgets of low-acceptance agents and reallocates reclaimed hardware budgets to accelerate the most predictable ones. This highly responsive mechanism ensures that the autoregressive drafting phase perfectly mirrors the underlying workload dynamics. Under the static and uniform budget allocation, hardware budgets are frequently wasted generating deep draft sequences for unpredictable, hard-to-draft workloads, which are ultimately rejected during the parallel verification phase. By preemptively suppressing these unproductive drafts and allocate draft budget to high-yield targets, our scheduler maximizes the effective accepted tokens per verification step. The lower panel of Figure 13 illustrates this efficiency gain by plotting cumulative generated tokens against wall-clock time. By eliminating speculative computational waste, the dynamic policy achieves a strictly steeper generation trajectory compared to the baseline. For an identical workload output of 881 881 target tokens, this continuous reallocation reduces the total execution time from 434 434 seconds to 388 388 seconds. This translates to a 1.12 × 1.12\times end-to-end speedup, demonstrating that HAL-guided dynamic budget allocation is fundamentally critical for optimizing concurrent multi-agent inference. 4.5. Stall-Aware Context Switching To evaluate system resilience against tool-induced stalls, we benchmark our asynchronous yielding mechanism using three concurrent agents. Under standard synchronous execution, tool invocations critically block active execution streams. As depicted in the upper timeline of Figure 14 , waiting for external processes (such as script execution and API responses) forces the hardware into extended idle states, clearly illustrated by Agent B suffering a prolonged 53-second stall. These synchronous execution stalls entirely serialize external latency and tensor computation, severely degrading overall system efficiency. Our stall-aware runtime eliminates this computational waste. Upon initiating an external tool request, the active agent suspends its execution context and yields the hardware. As shown via the interleaved scheduling paths in the lower timeline of Figure 14 , when Agent B blocks, the global scheduler instantly promotes Agent A or Agent C. Allowing companion agents to steal these idle budgets achieves deep overlap between tensor computation and tool execution. As quantified in the right panels of Figure 14 , this dense execution packing reduces the end-to-end wall-clock time from 286 to 238 seconds and elevates global throughput from 9.9 to 11.4 tokens per second, ensuring continuous hardware saturation despite highly irregular tool invocations. 5. Related Work LLM Serving for Agentic Workloads. The shift to ReAct-style agents ( Yao et al., 2023 ) shatters the continuous batching assumptions of traditional runtimes like vLLM ( vLLM Project, 2024 ) . To support complex control flows, SGLang ( SGLang Team, 2024 ) and AgentInfer ( Lin et al., 2025 ) co-design runtime memory with application semantics, while Continuum ( Li et al., 2025b ) and INFERCEPT ( Abhyankar et al., 2024 ) mitigate tool-induced stalls via cache retention and KV swapping. However, these mechanisms target discrete GPUs. In edge unified memory architectures (UMA), such heavy-handed state management is obsolete. EdgeAgent exploits UMA for in-place KV metadata freezing, achieving zero-overhead context switching without moving physical bytes. Dynamic Speculative Scheduling. Recent algorithms push acceptance rates via training-time testing (EAGLE-3 ( Li et al., 2025d ) ) and pipelined SSM voting (Smurfs ( Wang et al., 2025 ) ). System-level designs tailor speculation budgets to specific constraints: AdaServe ( Li et al., 2025a ) optimizes for cloud SLOs, EdgeLLM ( Xu et al., 2025 ) adapts draft-tree width for memory-constrained devices, and Ghidorah ( Wei et al., 2025a ) partitions verification across edge cores. For agents, DualSpec ( Zhong et al., 2026 ) utilizes semantic critics, and AgentInfer ( Lin et al., 2025 ) leverages suffix automata. Unlike these coarse-grained or static allocations, EdgeAgent uses the HAL as an effective indicator of drafting difficulty to dynamically allocate budgets across concurrent multi-agent streams. Heterogeneous Execution on Edge SoCs. To harness disparate edge compute units, HeteroInfer ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , Doppeladler ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) , and earlier vision frameworks ( Li et al., 2025c ) predict workload split ratios across heterogeneous processing units. Concurrently, Hello SME! ( Remke and Breuer, 2024 ) and MPGEMM ( Deng et al., 2025 ) optimize standalone GEMM micro-kernels for ARM SME architectures. However, the former execution frameworks rely on per-operator runtime heuristics without whole-graph analysis, while the latter isolated libraries lack end-to-end integration. EdgeAgent bridges this gap via a logical DAG topology barrier, enabling lock-free, zero-copy tensor routing to saturate asymmetric cores without runtime restructuring. Generalizability beyond UMA. EdgeAgent’s two layers have different portability. The agent-aware scheduling layer is memory-topology-agnostic: HAL-based budget allocation and suspend-and-yield operate on runtime state (drafting difficulty and tool-stall events), which exists in any speculative-decoding system. They therefore transfer unchanged to discrete-GPU datacenters, where tool-induced stalls cause the same slot-wasting and head-of-line blocking problem. The UMA-aware execution layer, in contrast, derives its benefit specifically from the coherent shared address space: on a discrete GPU over PCIe the disjoint-write trick cannot remove the host–device transfer, although the same principle, partitioning by device throughput and synchronizing only on completion, maps to multi-GPU tensor parallelism over high-bandwidth interconnects or to CPU-offload schemes such as FlexGen ( Sheng et al., 2023 ) , where the goal becomes minimizing PCIe traffic and overlapping compute with transfers. Finally, the ARM SME micro-kernels are a backend accelerator rather than an architectural dependency: they speed up the CPU shard but are not required for correctness, and equivalent tiled kernels exist for x86 AMX and NVIDIA Tensor Cores. 6. Conclusion We propose EdgeAgent , a cross-layer inference system that tightly couples agent-aware scheduling with hardware-level execution to meet the demands of concurrent multi-agent LLM workflows on edge UMA devices. By leveraging agent-aware dynamic budgeting, stall-aware suspend-and-yield mechanisms, and zero-copy architecture-aware tensor parallelism, EdgeAgent largely improves hardware utilization even under highly irregular execution patterns. Our design illustrates the necessity of end-to-end co-design across semantic and physical layers for efficient, real-time agentic AI, paving the way for future intelligent edge systems.
